newsitem.title: USA: US bonds take wait-and-see approach to budget pact.
newsitem.headline: US bonds take wait-and-see approach to budget pact.

text.p: As talk of a U.S. budget agreement increases, Treasury market participants remain cautious about factoring in an accord at this time, especially after being burned in early 1996.
The market is more preoccupied with the economy and whether it is growing fast enough to spur inflation and force the Federal Reserve into an interest rate hike in the months ahead.
"At this moment, (the budget issue) is playing second fiddle," said Neil DeSarno, head government bond trader at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp. "People are more worried about inflation."
In recent days, administration and Congressional officials have repeated campaign promises for a bipartisan agreement to balance the budget by 2002.

A year or so ago, talk like that would probably have ignited a Treasury market rally. In fact, anticipation of a budget agreement in late 1995 and early 1996 -- as well as fear of recession and subsequent rate cuts -- pushed 30-year bond yields below 6.0 percent.
When budget talks fell apart following partisan politics resulting in two government shutdowns, bond yields jumped more than 40 basis points between mid-January and mid-February of last year.

"After years of rising frustration...something significant is finally happening," Rep. John Spratt, the chief Democrat on the House Budget Committee, said on Thursday. "I am optimistic we will do it this year. We are closer to the goal that we've ever been in 15 years."
Later Thursday, House Speaker Newt Gingrich said he was hopeful of reaching a budget pact with President Clinton.

"Our forecast assumes an agreement reached by the end of the year, but the bond market won't react to it until June or July when issues come forth and are being dealt with in a constructive way," said Bill Sharp, an economist at Smith Barney Inc.
Assuming a budget agreement, Sharp said he predicts the 30-year bond falling to 6.0 to 6.25 percent and the two-year note to 5.50 percent by the end of 1997.
Sharp said that a year ago the budget was the topic of discussion at every meeting and every conference call. "Now, maybe I get one question a week on it," he said.

David Jones, chief economist at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co, said that part of the big rally which took place after the November presidential elections was tied to the market's perception that Republicans and Democrats would finally get down to business in reaching a budget deficit agreement.

"The market was wildly optimistic," Jones said. But he remained skeptical, predicting that ethics issues and other Washington scandals should overshadow debate on any "fundamental structural reform on the budget that would produce credible deficit results."
Most, however, expect a budget compromise in 1997.

Still, economists figure there is a much better chance for a deal this time around, because House Speaker Newt Gingrich's influence has been weakened by ethics problems and he might be more receptive to compromise, and also because President Clinton is not running for re-election this year and has less reason to block a deal.

"What has changed from last year is Republicans are less ambitious about pushing their own agenda because the all-out push failed last year," said Lou Crandall, chief economist at R.H. Wrightson & Associates. "There is more likely something to come out of Congress that will be acceptable to the administration this time around.
"But," he added, "I don't see anything concrete enough to get the market excited about before the summer. And it is obviously uncertain that even in the summer the market will get excited."

"The assumption in the markets is that budget policy will remain, at worst, unchanged from current plans, which is broadly neutral," noted John Lipsky, chief economist at Chase Manhattan Bank NA. "I doubt if investors suspect there will be dramatic and shocking policy change. So investors will take a wait and see attitude on this."
The budget issue will eventually come into play, analysts said, but for now the market appears preooccupied with more immediate issues.
"The budget is a non-issue for right now," said Alan Levenson, money market economist at UBS Securities LLC. "The market is just trying to find out where the economy is going."
((-- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867))
